content: 1. Norfloxacin, like other fluoroquinolones, is associated with an increased risk of tendinitis and tendon rupture across all age groups. The Achilles tendon is most commonly affected, and ruptures may require surgical intervention. Tendon injuries have also been reported in other areas, such as the rotator cuff, hand, biceps, and thumb. 2. The risk of tendinitis and tendon rupture is higher in patients over 60 years of age, those taking corticosteroids, and individuals with kidney, heart, or lung transplants. Additional risk factors include strenuous physical activity, renal failure, and pre-existing tendon disorders like rheumatoid arthritis. 3. Tendon injuries can occur during or after therapy, with some cases reported months after completing treatment. Norfloxacin should be discontinued immediately if a patient experiences pain, swelling, inflammation, or tendon rupture. Patients should rest and consult their healthcare provider about switching to a non-quinolone antimicrobial agent. 4. Fluoroquinolones, including norfloxacin, can exacerbate muscle weakness in patients with myasthenia gravis due to their neuromuscular blocking activity. Serious adverse events, including deaths and ventilatory support requirements, have been reported in such patients. Norfloxacin should be avoided in individuals with a history of myasthenia gravis. 5. The safety and efficacy of oral norfloxacin in pediatric patients, adolescents under 18, pregnant women, and nursing mothers have not been established. Animal studies have shown cartilage damage in immature animals exposed to high doses of norfloxacin. 6. Norfloxacin has been associated with central nervous system (CNS) effects, including seizures, increased intracranial pressure, toxic psychosis, tremors, restlessness, confusion, and hallucinations. If these occur, the drug should be discontinued, and appropriate measures should be taken. Caution is advised in patients with known or suspected CNS disorders, such as epilepsy or severe cerebral arteriosclerosis. 7. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with quinolone therapy, sometimes after the first dose. Symptoms may include cardiovascular collapse, loss of consciousness, facial or pharyngeal edema, and urticaria. Immediate emergency treatment, including epinephrine, oxygen, and airway management, is required for severe reactions. 8. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including norfloxacin. CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile should be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. 9. Peripheral neuropathy, including sensory or sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy, has been reported with fluoroquinolones. Symptoms such as pain, burning, tingling, numbness, or weakness may occur soon after starting therapy and may be irreversible. Norfloxacin should be discontinued immediately if these symptoms develop. 10. Norfloxacin is not effective in treating syphilis. High-dose, short-term antimicrobial therapy for gonorrhea may mask or delay symptoms of incubating syphilis. Patients with gonorrhea should undergo serologic testing for syphilis at diagnosis and follow-up testing after three months. 11. Needle-shaped crystals have been observed in the urine of volunteers receiving high doses of norfloxacin. To minimize this risk, patients should not exceed the recommended daily dose and should maintain adequate hydration and urinary output. 12. Norfloxacin may cause photosensitivity or phototoxicity, leading to skin reactions after sun or UV light exposure. Patients should avoid excessive light exposure and discontinue the drug if phototoxicity occurs. 13. Rarely, hemolytic reactions have been reported in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency taking quinolones. Caution is advised in such patients. 14. Norfloxacin should only be prescribed for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections to avoid the development of drug-resistant bacteria. Patients should complete the full course of therapy as directed to ensure effectiveness and reduce the risk of resistance. 15. Periodic assessment of organ function, including renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic systems, is recommended during prolonged therapy with norfloxacin. 16. Norfloxacin has not shown carcinogenic or mutagenic effects in animal studies. It did not adversely affect fertility in male and female mice at high doses. 17. Norfloxacin is classified as Pregnancy Category C. It has been shown to cause embryonic loss in monkeys at high doses but has not demonstrated teratogenic effects in animal studies. It should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 18. It is unknown whether norfloxacin is excreted in human milk. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. 19. The safety and efficacy of norfloxacin in pediatric patients and adolescents under 18 years of age have not been established. Norfloxacin has been shown to cause arthropathy in juvenile animals. 20. Elderly patients are at increased risk of severe tendon disorders, including tendon rupture, especially when taking corticosteroids. Caution should be exercised when prescribing norfloxacin to elderly patients, and renal function should be monitored due to the drug's excretion by the kidneys. 21. Norfloxacin may prolong the QTc interval on an electrocardiogram. Caution is advised in patients with known QTc prolongation, uncorrected hypokalemia, or those taking drugs that affect the QTc interval. 22. Patients should be informed about the potential side effects of norfloxacin, including tendon disorders, CNS effects, hypersensitivity reactions, photosensitivity, and peripheral neuropathy. They should be advised to contact their healthcare provider if any concerning symptoms occur.
